name: 5259 BC Solar Particle Event

phenomena.details: Average Delta-14C jump of +19.1 (+/-0.6) per mil within ~2 years across four absolutely dated tree-ring chronologies; modelled production spike ~0.3 yr.

impacts.description: Brief, intense solar energetic particle event driving a sharp rise in atmospheric radiocarbon production worldwide.
Prehistoric event with no written record; detected only through tree-ring radiocarbon.

papers.title: Tree-rings reveal two strong solar proton events in 7176 and 5259 BCE
papers.authors: Brehm, N., Christl, M., Knowles, T. D. J., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Identified a +19.1 per mil radiocarbon spike at 5259 BCE across chronologies from Switzerland/Germany, Ireland, Russia and the USA; after geomagnetic correction the event is similar to but slightly weaker than AD 775.

summary: A short, intense extreme solar particle event in 5259 BC, detected as a large radiocarbon spike across four independent, absolutely dated tree-ring chronologies, of magnitude similar to the AD 774 event.
description: Reported by Brehm et al. (2022), the 5259 BCE event appears as an average Delta-14C increase of +19.1 (+/-0.6) per mil within about two years, measured in absolutely dated tree-ring chronologies from Switzerland/Germany, Ireland, Russia and the United States. Its 14C excess mass (29.2 +/-0.9 kg) is marginally larger than that of AD 775 (26.2 +/-1.0 kg) in raw terms, but after accounting for the weaker contemporaneous geomagnetic field the event is judged similar to, but slightly weaker than, the AD 774/775 benchmark. The modelled production spike of roughly 0.3 years is far shorter than the annual sampling, consistent with a single brief extreme solar eruption. Unlike 660 BC and 7176 BC, no high-resolution ice-core 10Be/36Cl confirmation has yet been published, so the solar origin rests on the global synchroneity of the tree-ring signal.
